design_detail: Secondary analysis of wave 1 (2001–2002) of the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC), a US national multistage probability survey of civilian non-institutionalized adults living in households and group quarters, interviewed face to face by Census Bureau interviewers with the AUDADIS-IV (response 81%). Of 43,093 respondents, the 3,297 with lifetime DSM-IV cannabis use disorder (abuse, dependence or both; 2,080 men and 1,217 women) were compared by gender on sociodemographic characteristics, lifetime psychiatric disorders, the course of the disorder (recalled ages at first use, heavy use, onset and remission; criteria; episodes) and help seeking. Weighted percentages and means with design-based standard errors (SUDAAN); comorbidity also modelled in the whole sample with gender, lifetime cannabis use disorder and their interaction. A general-population sample, not a treatment sample.
can_establish: How US adults who had ever met DSM-IV criteria for cannabis abuse or dependence by 2001–2002 differed by gender in their recalled ages at first use and onset, lifetime comorbidity, criteria met, recalled remission and ever seeking help.
cannot_establish: Whether women progress to cannabis use disorder faster than men in any general sense (the comparison is among people who already had the disorder, unadjusted for current age, from ages recalled at one interview); whether the disorder causes or follows the comorbid disorders (cross-sectional); or how remission relates to treatment (remission is not defined and not crossed with help seeking).

sample.recruitment: General-population sample: NESARC 2001–2002, US civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18 and older living in households and group quarters (shelters and group homes included, per the Discussion); Black and Hispanic people and young adults (18–24) oversampled; data weighted for oversampling and non-response and to the 2000 census; response rate 81% (PDF p. 2, 2.1 Sample; PDF p. 6, Discussion, 9th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Respondents with lifetime DSM-IV cannabis abuse, dependence or both by AUDADIS-IV (PDF p. 2, 2.1 Sample). How many had dependence and how many abuse only is not reported.
sample.demographics: Table 1 (PDF p. 3), men vs women with the disorder, weighted %: aged 18–29 29.19 vs 35.82; 30–44 42.15 vs 43.05; over 45 28.66 vs 21.13; White 77.13 vs 78.54; Black 9.90 vs 9.10; Hispanic 7.67 vs 6.99; college education 55.51 vs 64.18; personal income under $20,000 35.74 vs 58.74; employed 81.15 vs 69.34; married 54.74 vs 52.98; widowed or divorced 14.17 vs 19.26.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one interview). Item-level missing data are not reported; Tables 2 to 4 print the full group sizes for every row, including rows that apply only to subgroups (see reporting issues).
sample.selection_effects: General-population survey; people in institutions and homeless people outside shelters are not sampled, which the authors note may miss some people with the disorder (PDF p. 6). The comparison is restricted to people who had the disorder, so the time from first use to onset says nothing about the chance of developing it, which the authors cite as about twice as high in men (11.8% vs 5.4% lifetime, from Stinson et al., 2006; PDF p. 2). Women with the disorder were younger (Table 1), and younger respondents can only report short intervals between first use and onset.

exposure.measurement: The groups compared are men and women (the paper uses 'gender' and does not separate biological sex from social roles). Ages at first cannabis use, at heavy use (daily, or more than 20 days a month), at onset of the disorder and at remission were self-reported at the single interview; nothing was recorded as it happened (PDF p. 2, 2.2 Measures, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Average joints a day during the period of heaviest use: men 3.38 (SE 0.12) vs women 2.54 (0.12); duration of the longest episode 40.43 (2.09) vs 31.01 (2.10) months (Table 3, PDF p. 4). Other routes not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Other substance use disorders are reported as comorbidities (Table 2, PDF p. 4): any other substance use disorder 92.22% of men vs 88.39% of women, alcohol use disorder 84.97 vs 74.56%, any other drug use disorder 41.60 vs 37.34%, nicotine dependence 50.93 vs 52.73%. None was adjusted for in the course, remission or help-seeking comparisons.

comparison.controls: Men compared with women among people with the disorder; for comorbidity, people without the disorder in the whole NESARC sample also enter the interaction models.
comparison.matching: None. Course, remission and help-seeking comparisons are unadjusted (weighted means and percentages with Wald F tests or odds ratios); comorbidity models adjusted for ethnicity, nativity, age, education, personal income, employment, marital status, urbanicity and region (Table 2, footnote c, PDF p. 4).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history, childhood adversity, the timing of the comorbid disorders and other drug use before cannabis were not used; conduct problems appear only as lifetime conduct disorder. Current age was not adjusted for in the course comparisons although women with the disorder were younger.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable to the gender comparison; see polysubstance.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS-IV: DSM-IV cannabis abuse criteria rated independently of dependence; mood, anxiety and personality disorders. Course questions: ages at first use, heavy use, onset and remission; number of episodes; criteria met; duration of the longest episode; joints a day. Help seeking grouped as professional treatment (outpatient visits; inpatient detoxification or rehabilitation unit or hospital ward; emergency department) or help from human service professionals (clergy, employee assistance programmes, family or social services, halfway houses, therapeutic communities, crisis centres, self-help groups); reasons for not seeking help in four groups (PDF p. 2, 2.2 Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite well-documented reliability and validity of AUDADIS substance use disorder diagnoses and fair-to-good test-retest reliability (κ 0.40–0.62) of the mood, anxiety and personality diagnoses (PDF p. 2). The reliability of the recalled ages is not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Telescoping = time from age at first cannabis use to age at onset of the disorder, compared between men and women who had the disorder (PDF p. 2, 2.2 Measures, 4th paragraph). Remission is not defined. Whether the help-seeking questions asked about help for cannabis specifically is not stated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Two percentages were treated as different when the 95% CI of their odds ratio excluded 1 (PDF p. 2, 2.3 Statistical analyses, 3rd paragraph). About 52 outcomes were compared (30 comorbidity rows, each with two odds ratios; 12 course rows; 10 help-seeking rows; editors' count), besides 11 sociodemographic characteristics.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (lay interviewers knew respondents' gender).

analysis.effect_sizes: Course (Table 3, PDF p. 4), men vs women, weighted means (SE): age at first use 16.71 (0.10) vs 16.73 (0.12), Wald F 0.02, p 0.8768; age at heavy use 18.15 (0.16) vs 18.28 (0.25), p 0.6676; age at onset 19.34 (0.13) vs 18.98 (0.16), F 2.73, p 0.1035; time from first use to onset 2.64 (0.10) vs 2.24 (0.13) years, F 5.20, p 0.0259; abuse criteria 1.62 vs 1.49, p 0.0005; dependence criteria 4.23 vs 4.20, p 0.7982; longest episode 40.43 vs 31.01 months, p 0.0009; age at remission 25.32 vs 23.08, F 48.45, p < 0.0001; remitted 77.83% vs 82.10%, OR 0.77 (0.62–0.95). Help seeking (Table 4, PDF p. 5): any 14.20% vs 12.43%, OR 1.17 (0.92–1.48); no type of help or reason for not seeking help differed. Comorbidity (Table 2): see key findings. Editors' calculation: the difference in time to onset is 0.40 years (about 5 months), approximate 95% CI 0.08 to 0.72 years from the printed SEs (ignoring covariance); no SD is printed, so no standardized difference can be computed.
analysis.covariates: None for the course, remission and help-seeking comparisons. Comorbidity models: gender, lifetime cannabis use disorder, their interaction, ethnicity, nativity, age, education, personal income, employment status, marital status, urbanicity and region (Table 2, footnote c).
analysis.selective_reporting: The proportions with abuse only and with dependence are not reported; the analysed numbers for Table 3 rows that apply to subgroups are not given; the model behind the 'gender main effect' column is explained only in footnotes, and the within-disorder gender odds ratios the text describes are not shown.
analysis.power: Not reported. 1,217 women and 2,080 men; the reasons for not seeking help rest on a much smaller, unreported subgroup (see reporting issues).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among US adults with a lifetime cannabis use disorder in 2001–2002, men and women had started cannabis at the same age (16.7 years) and the disorder had begun at similar ages (19.3 vs 19.0 years, p = 0.10); the recalled interval from first use to onset was 0.40 years shorter in women (2.24 vs 2.64 years, p = 0.026, unadjusted). Men met more abuse criteria, used more joints a day, had longer episodes and were older at remission; more women than men reported remission (82.1 vs 77.8%). About one in seven had ever sought help, with no gender difference. Among people with the disorder, men more often had other substance use disorders and antisocial personality disorder and women more often mood and anxiety disorders; some psychiatric disorder was nearly universal in both (95.6 vs 94.1%), largely because other substance use disorders, including nicotine dependence, were counted.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that men with the disorder were more likely than women to have any psychiatric disorder, that after adjustment women with the disorder were at greater risk for externalizing disorders, and that "Women experienced telescoping to CUD" (PDF p. 1); the Discussion calls this evidence for the telescoping phenomenon, suggests gender-specific pathways (PDF p. 6), and reads the remission figures as possibly showing that the disorder remits naturally for a high proportion of people (PDF p. 6). Gaps: (1) by the table footnotes, the 'gender main effect' odds ratios that the text gives for men vs women with the disorder come from a whole-sample model with an interaction term; multiplied by the interaction odds ratios they reproduce the crude odds ratios among people with the disorder (editors' check), and among people with the disorder the difference in any psychiatric disorder is not significant by the printed SEs; (2) interaction odds ratios below 1 mean that the male excess in these disorders is smaller among people with the disorder than among people without it, not that women with the disorder had them more often: men with the disorder had the higher percentages of other substance use disorders, alcohol use disorder, pathological gambling and antisocial personality disorder; (3) telescoping rests on a 5-month difference, unadjusted for current age although women were younger, conditional on having the disorder, from recalled ages, among about 50 comparisons without correction, while the age at onset itself did not differ; (4) remission is undefined and not related to help seeking, so it cannot show remission without treatment. The limitations paragraph names self-report and the cross-sectional design, but not the recall of ages or the lack of age adjustment.

timeline.event: Project MATCH alcohol treatment sample, cited by the authors as clinical evidence of telescoping (read in this round: shorter recalled intervals in women for two of three landmark pairs and to first treatment, mainly in older participants).

Hernandez-Avila, Rounsaville and Kranzler: women entering treatment for opioid, cannabis or alcohol dependence progressed faster to treatment; one of the two earlier, small studies of telescoping in cannabis dependence cited by the authors (PDF p. 2).
Ehlers et al., San Francisco Family Study: the other earlier study of telescoping in cannabis dependence cited by the authors (PDF p. 2).
The authors' group's general-population analysis of alcohol dependence, cited as indicating that telescoping may not occur in general-population samples (PDF p. 6).
This study: NESARC general-population sample; recalled time from first cannabis use to onset 0.40 years shorter in women, unadjusted, among people with the disorder.

Critique describes this study as finding a time from first cannabis use to the disorder 2.5 years shorter in women (as recorded on the library's card sc_marks_2018); the primary paper gives 2.64 vs 2.24 years, a difference of 0.40 years.

replication.where_it_stands: This is the general-population cannabis analysis that later reviews cite for telescoping. Read in full, it shows a small (0.40-year) unadjusted difference in the recalled time from first use to onset among people who had the disorder, with no difference in the age at onset itself; the same research group's alcohol analysis of two national surveys (keyes_2010) did not find the full pattern. The description of this study as a 2.5-year difference (Marks and Clark, as recorded on sc_marks_2018) does not match the paper. No re-analysis adjusting for age or birth cohort, or separating the chance of developing the disorder from the speed, is cited here.

funding.funder: Role of funding source: NESARC was funded by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (Bethesda, MD), with supplemental support from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (Bethesda). Work on the manuscript: NIH grants DA019606-S3 and DA020783-S4 (printed as 'MR Khan'); DA019606, DA023200, DA023973 and CA133050 (Dr. Blanco); the New York State Psychiatric Institute (Dr. Blanco); Spanish Ministry of Education grant PR2010-0501 (Dr. Secades-Villa) (PDF p. 6).
funding.declared_conflicts: Conflict of interest: no conflict declared (PDF p. 6).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, Columbia University/New York State Psychiatric Institute (Khan, Secades-Villa, Okuda, Wang, Pérez-Fuentes, Blanco); Department of Psychology, University of Oviedo (Secades-Villa); Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Maryland (Kerridge) (PDF p. 1). Contributors: Blanco designed the study; Khan and Secades-Villa managed the literature searches and wrote the first draft; Wang ran the analyses (PDF p. 6). No commercial interest is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of young women and men followed from before first cannabis use, with use, criteria and help seeking recorded as they happen, analysed so as to separate the chance of developing the disorder from the speed of developing it and adjusted for age and birth cohort; and a re-analysis of the NESARC data with survival methods that censor at current age.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: National probability frame of civilian non-institutionalized adults, including group quarters; institutions and homeless people outside shelters are not covered.
Multistage probability sampling with oversampling and weights; design-based standard errors (SUDAAN).

3,297 people with the disorder (1,217 women); but the reasons for not seeking help rest on an unreported subgroup whose standard errors imply only about 100 to 180 effective respondents (editors' inference).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives the sociodemographic profile by gender; the survey design is described by reference.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Item missingness not reported; full group sizes printed for rows that apply only to subgroups.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: DSM-IV diagnoses by a structured interview with cited reliability; but the course measures behind the telescoping and remission findings are recalled ages, and remission is not defined.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants

domains.note: Weighted, design-based analyses are appropriate, but the course comparisons are unadjusted for current age although women were younger, there is no correction for multiple comparisons, and the comorbidity odds ratios are presented as within-disorder differences although they come from a whole-sample interaction model.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI has no overall algorithm; the editors' summary is moderate risk. The weighted percentages and means by gender among people with the disorder (Tables 1 to 4) come from a large national probability sample with good response and a standard interview, and can be cited as descriptions of US adults with a lifetime cannabis use disorder in 2001–2002. The analytic statements are weaker: the telescoping finding is a 5-month unadjusted difference among people who already had the disorder, from recalled ages; remission is undefined; and the text's gender odds ratios for comorbidity describe people without the disorder. Cite the paper for the percentages, for the absence of differences in ages at first use and onset, for the small difference in recalled interval, and for low and similar rates of help seeking; do not cite it as showing that women progress faster to cannabis use disorder, that women with the disorder have more externalizing disorders than men with it, or that the disorder remits without treatment.

key_findings.finding: NESARC 2001–2002: face-to-face Census Bureau interviews with 43,093 US civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18 and older in households and group quarters, response rate 81%, oversampling of Black and Hispanic people and young adults, weighted to the 2000 census. The study sample was the 2,080 men and 1,217 women with lifetime DSM-IV cannabis abuse, dependence or both (AUDADIS-IV).
key_findings.page: PDF p. 2 of the in-press version

key_findings.finding: Women with the disorder were younger than men with it (aged 18–29: 35.82% vs 29.19%; over 45: 21.13% vs 28.66%; OR for men 1.66, 95% CI 1.34–2.06 for over 45 vs 18–29), more often had a college education (64.18% vs 55.51%), more often had an income under $20,000 (58.74% vs 35.74%), and were less often employed (69.34% vs 81.15%).
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 2–3 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Sociodemographic characteristics, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2); Table 1 (PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Men and women with the disorder did not differ in recalled age at first cannabis use (16.71, SE 0.10, vs 16.73, SE 0.12; Wald F 0.02, p 0.8768), at heavy use (18.15 vs 18.28; p 0.6676) or at onset of the disorder (19.34, SE 0.13, vs 18.98, SE 0.16; F 2.73, p 0.1035). The recalled time from first use to onset was 2.64 years (SE 0.10) in men and 2.24 (SE 0.13) in women (F 5.20, p 0.0259), which the authors present as evidence of telescoping. Editors' calculation: difference 0.40 years, about 5 months (approximate 95% CI 0.08 to 0.72), unadjusted for current age or anything else.
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 3–4 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Clinical characteristics and course, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 3 (PDF p. 4)
key_findings.note: General-population sample; all ages recalled at one interview; comparison restricted to people who had the disorder.

key_findings.finding: Men with the disorder met more abuse criteria (mean 1.62 vs 1.49; F 13.66, p 0.0005), smoked more joints a day during their heaviest use (3.38 vs 2.54; F 30.84, p < 0.0001) and had longer episodes (40.43 vs 31.01 months; F 12.04, p 0.0009); dependence criteria (4.23 vs 4.20) and numbers of episodes did not differ.
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 3–4 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Clinical characteristics and course, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 3 (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Remission was reported by 77.83% (SE 1.13) of men and 82.10% (1.28) of women (OR for men 0.77, 95% CI 0.62–0.95); mean age at remission was 25.32 vs 23.08 years (F 48.45, p < 0.0001). Remission is not defined in the paper, the window is lifetime to the interview, and remission is not reported by help seeking.
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 2–4 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 2.2 Measures, 4th paragraph (PDF p. 2); 3.3, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 3 (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Help seeking was low and similar: any treatment 14.20% (SE 0.98) of men vs 12.43% (1.03) of women (OR 1.17, 0.92–1.48); professional treatment 12.45% vs 11.16%; outpatient 9.53% vs 9.66%; inpatient 9.27% vs 7.03% (OR 1.35, 0.98–1.86); emergency room 3.11% vs 2.95%; human service professionals 11.44% vs 9.57%. Reasons for not seeking help, men vs women: lack of motivation 75.92% vs 75.88%, stigma 40.05% vs 44.01%, logistical barriers 39.55% vs 38.92%, decreased perceived need (stopped alone or with help from friends or family) 20.26% vs 22.88%; none differed.
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 4–5 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Treatment-seeking behaviors, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4); Table 4 and footnotes (PDF p. 5)
key_findings.note: Whether the questions asked about help for cannabis specifically is not stated; the base for the reasons appears to be a small, unreported subgroup (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Lifetime disorders among people with cannabis use disorder, men vs women (weighted %): any psychiatric disorder 95.57 vs 94.14; any other substance use disorder 92.22 vs 88.39; alcohol use disorder 84.97 vs 74.56; any other drug use disorder 41.60 vs 37.34; nicotine dependence 50.93 vs 52.73; any mood disorder 30.58 vs 49.47; major depressive disorder 17.35 vs 28.12; any anxiety disorder 25.67 vs 40.16; antisocial personality disorder 21.10 vs 14.36; conduct disorder 1.92 vs 2.49; pathological gambling 1.58 vs 1.26.
key_findings.page: PDF p. 4 of the in-press version

key_findings.finding: The 'gender main effect' adjusted odds ratios (for example any psychiatric disorder 1.25, 95% CI 1.19–1.31; any other substance use disorder 2.18; alcohol use disorder 2.90; antisocial personality disorder 2.99; any mood disorder 0.49) come, by the table footnotes, from a whole-sample model containing gender, lifetime cannabis use disorder, their interaction and sociodemographic covariates, with women without the disorder as the reference; the text presents them as differences between men and women with the disorder. Editors' check: each main-effect odds ratio multiplied by its interaction odds ratio reproduces the crude odds ratio from the percentages among people with the disorder (any psychiatric disorder 1.25 × 1.08 = 1.35 vs 1.34; alcohol use disorder 2.90 × 0.67 = 1.94 vs 1.93; antisocial personality disorder 2.99 × 0.53 = 1.58 vs 1.59), so the main effects describe men and women without the disorder. Among people with the disorder, 95.57% vs 94.14% (SEs 0.53 and 0.85) is not a significant difference (z about 1.4, ignoring covariance).
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 2–4 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Psychiatric comorbidity, 1st paragraph (starting PDF p. 2); Table 2 and footnotes a–c (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Gender × disorder interaction odds ratios were below 1 for any other substance use disorder (0.71, 0.54–0.94), alcohol use disorder (0.67, 0.53–0.83), nicotine dependence (0.77, 0.63–0.93), bipolar I and II (0.74, 0.58–0.95), conduct disorder (0.29, 0.15–0.58), pathological gambling (0.41, 0.17–0.96) and antisocial personality disorder (0.53, 0.40–0.71). The authors read these as women with the disorder being more likely than men to have these disorders (externalizing disorders in the abstract). In the editors' reading they mean the male excess seen in people without the disorder is smaller, on the odds scale, among people with it; among people with the disorder, men still had the higher percentages of other substance use disorders, alcohol use disorder, pathological gambling and antisocial personality disorder (Table 2).
key_findings.page: PDF pp. 3–4 of the in-press version
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Psychiatric comorbidity, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 3); Table 2 (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: The authors note that their group's general-population analysis of alcohol dependence (Keyes et al., 2010) indicated that telescoping may not occur in general-population samples, and suggest sample- and substance-specific aspects of telescoping; they offer gender differences in reinforcement or the role of comorbidity as possible causes, untested here.
key_findings.page: PDF p. 6 of the in-press version

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: self-report not confirmed by other informants; cross-sectional design; household surveys may miss some people with the disorder (shelters and group homes were sampled); some disorders, such as obsessive-compulsive disorder, not assessed.
key_findings.page: PDF p. 6 of the in-press version

reporting_issues.issue: The 'gender main effect' odds ratios in Table 2 are, by footnotes a–c, from a whole-sample model with a gender × disorder interaction, so they compare men and women without the disorder; the Results (3.2, 1st paragraph) and the abstract present them as differences between men and women with the disorder.
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 1–4 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement that men with the disorder were more likely than women to have any psychiatric disorder is not supported by the within-disorder percentages (95.57% vs 94.14%); cite the percentages, not the main-effect odds ratios, for gender differences among people with the disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: Interaction odds ratios below 1 are described as women with the disorder being more likely than men to have the disorders concerned (PDF p. 3) and as women being at greater risk for externalizing disorders (PDF p. 1), although the within-disorder percentages are higher in men for most of these disorders (Table 2).
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 1, 3–4 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: The finding should be cited as a stronger association of cannabis use disorder with these disorders in women than in men on the odds scale, not as more frequent disorders in women with cannabis use disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: Every row of Table 3 carries the full group sizes (2,080 and 1,217), although age at remission applies only to people who remitted and the episode and criteria counts apply to people with abuse or with dependence; footnote b (among people with abuse or dependence) also differs from the Methods (abuse criteria among people with abuse, dependence criteria among people with dependence).
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 2, 4 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysed numbers for these rows are unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Footnote d of Table 4 gives the base for the reasons for not seeking help as everyone who did not seek treatment (about 1,785 men and 1,066 women, editors' arithmetic), but the standard errors of these percentages (2.98 to 4.85 points) are three to five times those of the help-seeking rates (0.95 to 1.03), implying an effective base of only about 100 to 180 people per sex (editors' inference).
reporting_issues.page: PDF p. 5 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: The reasons apply to an unreported subgroup; their precision and generality are lower than the footnote suggests.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion supports natural remission, and remission taking several years, by citing Lopez-Quintero et al. (2011), whose title in the reference list concerns transition from first use to dependence, not remission.
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 6–7 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: The remission interpretation rests on a citation that, by its title, does not address remission.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor reporting points in this in-press version: Table 1 lists a 'Northwest' region alongside Midwest, South and West; Table 2 reports histrionic personality disorder, psychotic disorder, conduct disorder and pathological gambling, which the Methods list of assessed disorders does not mention; one Discussion sentence on alcohol telescoping is garbled.
reporting_issues.page: PDF pp. 2–3, 4, 6 of the in-press version
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the version of record (not read) may differ.

verification.source_read: In-press (article-in-press) PDF, 8 pages numbered 1–8, headed Drug and Alcohol Dependence xxx (2012) xxx–xxx; its pages differ from the version of record (Drug Alcohol Depend 130(1–3):101–108, 2013), which was not read; anchors give the PDF's own page numbers. All pages read; every number checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi and Tables 2 and 3 at 220 dpi; no supplement.
